Significance
 Mental health symptoms, 
including depression, are on the 
rise among young people. In a 
large US national 2-y longitudinal 
study of 9- to 11-y-old youth, we 
found evidence for a brain–
environment interaction in the 
development of depressive 
symptoms. Youth showed greater 
increases in depressive symptoms 
when they had experienced 
greater family conflict, greater 
depressive symptoms in their 
primary caregiver, less parental 
warmth, greater peer 
victimization, and a less prosocial 
school environment. These effects 
were amplified for youth with a 
larger left hippocampus. Thus, 
families, peers, and schools play 
an important role in the 
emergence of depressive 
symptoms during the transition to 
adolescence, and the left 
hippocampus is a brain structure 
that enhances sensitivity to these 
social contexts.

Depressive symptoms during the transition to adolescence: 
Left hippocampal volume as a marker of social context 
sensitivity
Matias Martineza,b,c

The transition to adolescence is a critical period for mental health development. 
Socio-­experiential environments play an important role in the emergence of depres-
sive symptoms with some adolescents showing more sensitivity to social contexts 
than others. Drawing on recent developmental neuroscience advances, we examined 
whether hippocampal volume amplifies social context effects in the transition to 
adolescence. We analyzed 2-­y longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive 
Development (ABCD®) study in a diverse sample of 11,832 youth (mean age: 9.914 
y; range: 8.917 to 11.083 y; 47.8% girls) from 21 sites across the United States. 
Socio-­experiential environments (i.e., family conflict, primary caregiver’s depressive 
symptoms, parental warmth, peer victimization, and prosocial school environment), 
hippocampal volume, and a wide range of demographic characteristics were measured 
at baseline. Youth’s symptoms of major depressive disorder were assessed at both 
baseline and 2 y later. Multilevel mixed-­effects linear regression analyses showed 
that negative social environments (i.e., family conflict, primary caregiver’s depressive 
symptoms, and peer victimization) and the absence of positive social environments 
(i.e., parental warmth and prosocial school environment) predicted greater increases in 
youth’s depressive symptoms over 2 y. Importantly, left hippocampal volume amplified 
social context effects such that youth with larger left hippocampal volume experienced 
greater increases in depressive symptoms in more negative and less positive social 
environments. Consistent with brain–environment interaction models of mental 
health, these findings underscore the importance of families, peers, and schools in 
the development of depression during the transition to adolescence and show how 
neural structure amplifies social context sensitivity.

 Depression is a leading cause of disability with over 300 million people living with it 
worldwide ( 1 ). The number of depression diagnoses ( 2 ) and associated economic costs 
( 3 ) have been on the rise during the past decades. Recent increases in serious psycho-
logical distress, depressive symptoms, and suicidal thoughts and attempts among young 
people in the United States specifically ( 4 ,  5 ) have worried policymakers, scholars, and 
laypeople alike.
 Adverse social experiences during childhood are one of the leading preventable or mod-
ifiable causes of depression and other mental health problems during adulthood ( 6 ,  7 ). 
However, it is less well understood how experiences in different social contexts ( 8 – 10 )—
families, peers, and schools—predict the emergence of depressive symptoms during the 
transition to adolescence, a developmental period of major reorganization across neural, 
cognitive, emotional, and social systems ( 11 ,  12 ). Moreover, major models of mental health 
development emphasize that some people are more sensitive than others to adverse social 
contexts ( 13 ,  14 ). These include diathesis-stress models, which propose that diatheses pre-
dispose individuals to developing mental health problems after negative experiences ( 15 , 
 16 ), resilience models that center on factors that lead individuals to withstand the adverse 
consequences of negative experiences ( 17 ,  18 ), as well as differential sensitivity, plasticity, 
or susceptibility models, which highlight individual differences in sensitivity to positive and 
negative environments with mental health consequences “for better or worse” ( 19 ,  20 ).
 Earlier empirical work focused on diathesis, resilience, or sensitivity factors across 
early-life temperamental traits (e.g., negative emotionality), genetic polymorphisms (e.g., 
5-HTTLPR genotype), and stress reactivity (e.g., cortisol responses to social stress) ( 20 ).

More recently, advances in developmental neuroscience have led 
researchers to develop brain–environment interaction models that 
seek to elucidate how differences in brain structure, functioning, 
and connectivity differentially shape sensitivity to social environ-
ments and attendant consequences for the development of psy-
chopathology ( 21 – 24 ).
 The hippocampus, a complex structure embedded deep into 
the temporal lobe ( 25 ), has been identified as a critical brain region 
involved in depression across the life span ( 26 ,  27 ). Emerging 
work suggests that one mechanism through which the hippocam-
pus plays a role in the development of depression is by enhancing 
social context sensitivity in adolescence ( 24 ,  28 ). The hippocam-
pus plays a fundamental role in making sense of the world around 
us and is essential in perception, imagination, recalling events, 
associative memory, spatial learning, emotional processing, affil-
iation, understanding social hierarchies, and transmitting contex-
tual information and representations to other brain regions 
involved in motivation and emotional regulation such as the 
amygdala, nucleus accumbens, medial prefrontal cortex, and ante-
rior cingulate ( 29 – 32 ). With high concentrations of glucocorti-
coid receptors and mineralocorticoid receptors, the hippocampus 
also plays a role in the glucocorticoid stress response. These recep-
tors (or transcription factors) allow the hippocampus to detect 
circulating glucocorticoids and exert an inhibitory effect on the 
hypothalamo–pituitary–adrenocortical (HPA) axis to terminate 
the stress response ( 33 – 35 ).
 Significant individual differences in hippocampal volume are 
observed across the lifespan. Numerous studies focused on the 
dynamic link between early life adversity, the stress response 
system, and hippocampal structure have shown a consistent 
reduction in adult hippocampal volume among those people 
who experienced early adversity ( 21 ,  22 ,  36 ). This association 
emerges several years after the onset of puberty, is thought to 
be mediated by a reduction in synaptogenesis and neurogenesis 
caused by prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids, appears to be 
stronger if exposure to adversity occurs before age 5, and may 
be unrelated to the development of mental health symptoms as 
smaller hippocampal volumes are also observed in resilient indi-
viduals to early life adversity without signs of psychopathology

( 6 ,  37 ,  38 ). Similarly, past studies on the link between positive 
environments and hippocampal structure report that larger 
hippocampal volumes are more common in individuals who 
grow up with more supportive mothers ( 39 ), perceive strong 
social support ( 40 ), have more empathic responses to an exper-
imenter’s displays of distress ( 41 ), engage in more diverse activ-
ities in a typical day ( 42 ), and report high levels of self-esteem 
( 43 ,  44 ). Moreover, a recent study of new fathers found signif-
icant growth in the left hippocampal volume between prenatal 
and postpartum time points, which was associated with stronger 
feelings of affectionate attachment, fewer bonding problems, 
and lower levels of dysfunctional parent–child interaction ( 45 ). 
Interestingly, hippocampal growth has also been observed after 
depressed individuals were treated with electroconvulsive ther-
apy ( 46 ) and increased hippocampal neurogenesis after the use 
of antidepressants ( 47 ). Overall, this evidence is consistent with 
animal models showing that hippocampal growth is typically 
promoted by enriched environments and related to increased 
neurogenesis, length and volume of myelinated fibers, long-term 
potentiation, density of dendritic arborization, and number of 
dendritic spines ( 48 – 50 ). According to multiple studies, the 
effects on hippocampal volume are typically lateralized and 
mainly manifest in the left hemisphere ( 6 ,  51 – 53 ). These 
left-lateralized hippocampal effects have been explained by an 
asymmetry of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor 
mediating the suppressive effects of glucocorticoids on hip-
pocampal neurogenesis ( 54 ,  55 ).
 Recent developmental neuroscience research suggests that hip-
pocampal volume can amplify sensitivity to social environments 
in the development of depressive symptoms during adolescence 
( 24 ,  56 ), as individuals’ biological systems may differentially 
respond to environmental demands ( 20 ,  24 ). Supporting this view, 
Whittle et al. ( 57 ) found an increase in depressive symptoms after 
exposure to maternal aggression among girls ages 11 to 15 with 
larger hippocampus, but not in girls with smaller hippocampal 
volume. Similarly, Schriber et al. ( 28 ) reported that high school 
students in grade 11 with larger left (but not right) hippocampal 
volume were more vulnerable to developing depressive symptoms 
if they lived in communities with high criminality and more resil-
ient if they experienced higher levels of family connectedness. 
Interestingly, emerging evidence has also shown that larger bilateral 
and left hippocampal volume measured within 1 mo after birth 
confers higher susceptibility to home quality environment and 
maternal sensitivity for cognitive and social development ( 58 ,  59 ).
 Drawing on differential sensitivity models ( 20 ) and brain–
environment interaction frameworks ( 24 ), the present study seeks 
to test whether the hippocampal volume amplifies sensitivity to 
negative and positive social contexts in the development of Major 
Depressive Disorder (MDD) symptoms during the transition to 
adolescence. This developmental stage marks a period of synaptic 
pruning and extensive myelination, making the brain more 
socially sensitive ( 20 ,  24 ). We analyzed 2-y longitudinal data 
from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study® 
(ABCD: abcdstudy.org )—a study aiming to follow the develop-
ment of around 11,800 adolescents ages 9 to 11 at the 2016 to 
2018 baseline for a decade ( 60 ,  61 ). Using this large database 
helps address limitations from previous studies such as small 
samples, cross-sectional measures, retrospective reports, and 
restrictions on the availability of potential confounders. Studies 
based on these data have already shown that the hippocampus is 
involved in the stress response system and mental health ( 62 – 67 ). 
To our knowledge, the present study is one of the few to take a 
brain–environment interaction approach to elucidate how the 
hippocampus amplifies sensitivity to social environments in the 
progression of depressive symptoms. The present study focused 
on social environments across three systems implicated in the 
development of depressive symptoms ( 8 – 10 )—family, peers, and 
schools—and examined both negative (i.e., peer victimization, 
family conflict, and primary caregiver’s depressive symptoms) 
and positive (i.e., prosocial school environments and parental 
warmth) social factors. In line with previous studies documenting

a left-lateralized effect ( 6 ,  51 – 53 ), we tested whether left hip-
pocampal volume moderates the link between 1) negative social 
contexts and the changes in MDD symptoms and 2) positive 
social contexts and the development of MDD symptoms. In 
follow-up analyses, we examined a) hemispheric specificity by 
examining right hippocampal volume as a moderator ( 28 ); b) 
specificity by sex at birth based on documented sex differences 
in the development of the hippocampus ( 68 – 70 ); c) alternative 
interpretations for the left hippocampal volume results by testing 
a role as meditator between social experiences and changes in 
MDD symptoms, a marker of depressive states, and scar of past 
depression; d) symptom heterogeneity and generalizability across 
individual MDD symptoms ( 71 ,  72 ); and e) specificity of the 
moderating effect to MDD symptoms by examining three other 
mental health symptoms: anxiety-related symptoms, psychotic- 
like experiences, and externalizing symptoms.

Results
Sample Demographics. The demographic characteristics of the 
11,832 youth (47.8% female) in the sample are summarized 
in SI Appendix, Table S1. The age at baseline was around 119 
mo old (9.914 y) with a range between 107 and 133 mo. Most 
participants were White (74.3%) and had a primary caregiver 
who attained a bachelor’s degree or higher (53.3%). The average 
number of symptoms of MDD was 0.413 at baseline and 0.314 at 
2-­y follow-­up. As shown in SI Appendix, Table S1, measurement of 
exposure to different social environments varies across experiences 
(peer victimization [PV] range [R] = 0 to 2, average [M] = 0.123, 
and SD = 0.283; family conflict [FC] R = 0-­1, M = 0.227, SD = 
0.217; primary caregiver’s depressive symptoms [PCDS] R = 5-­10, 
M = 5.403, SD = 0.599; prosocial school environment [PSE] R 
= 1-­4, M = 3.290, SD = 0.488; parental warmth [PW] R = 1-­3, 
M = 2.781, SD = 0.304).
Socio-­Experiential Environments Predict the Development of 
Depressive Symptoms. The longitudinal association between 
adverse social environments and the 2-­y change in MDD 
symptoms was positive after controlling for demographic 
characteristics (unstandardized [unstd] B = 0.266, P < 0.001 for 
PV; unstd B = 0.268, P < 0.001 for FC; unstd B = 0.106, P < 0.001 
for PCDS) and negative between positive social environments and 
MDD symptom development using the same model (unstd B = 
–0.106, P < 0.001 for PSE; unstd B = –0.222, P < 0.001 for PW). 
The associations between each social context and 2-­y change in 
MDD symptoms remained statistically significant (P < 0.05) when 
all environmental variables were included in the same regression 
model (Fig. 1).
 Due to differences in the nature, frequency, and degree of skew-
ness between the five socio-experiential variables, we did not 
attempt to compare the relative associations between these con-
texts and the 2-y change in MDD symptoms across environments. 
We conducted our analyses using the values from their original 
scales and focused on assessing the consistency, rather than com-
parability, of the moderating effects across social contexts. 
Demographic Covariates Predicted the Development of 
Depressive Symptoms. Some of the covariates included in the 
analysis significantly predicted the 2-­y change in MDD symptoms 
(SI  Appendix, Table  S2). Above and beyond, the longitudinal 
association between socio-­experiential environments and the 2-­y 
change in MDD, the following covariates measured at baseline also

predicted MDD changes in our linear mixed model: youth’s age 
[unstd B = 0.004, P = 0.021, following column (1) of SI Appendix, 
Table S2 as reference], youth’s sex at birth (unstd B = 0.228, P 
< 0.001), degree of pubertal development (unstd B = 0.107, P < 
0.001), lifetime experience of traumatic events (unstd B = 0.048, 
P = 0.002), parent’s history of depression (unstd B = 0.128, P = 
0.004), parent and grandparent’s history of depression (unstd B 
= 0.107, P = 0.006), whether the primary caregiver has a partner 
(unstd B = –0.087, P = 0.015), and the primary caregiver’s has 
master or PhD degree (unstd B = –0.097, P = 0.053, relative to 
caregivers who completed high school or less).
Negative Experiences Affect Youth with Larger Left Hippocampal 
Volumes. We examined whether the left hippocampal volume 
moderates the longitudinal association between MDD symptoms 
and three negative social contexts (i.e., PV, FC, and PCDS) 
by separately including a two-­way interaction between left 
hippocampal volume × socio-­experiential environments in three 
independent linear mixed models predicting MDD symptoms 
[Columns (1) to (3) in SI  Appendix, Table  S2]. These three 
interactions were positive and statistically significant (unstd B = 
0.980, P < 0.001 for PV; unstd B = 0.835, P = 0.003 for FC; unstd 
B = 0.258, P = 0.011 for PCDS). These results were robust when 
excluding covariates (see SI Appendix, Table S3; unstd B = 0.812, 
P < 0.001 for PV; unstd B = 0.683, P = 0.009 for FC; unstd B 
= 0.258, P = 0.006 for PCDS), conducting multiple imputation 
to handle missing values (see SI Appendix, Table S4; unstd B = 
0.584, P = 0.004 for PV; unstd B = 0.641, P = 0.019 for FC; 
unstd B = 0.207, P = 0.031 for PCDS), and using the square root 
transformation of symptoms as the outcome (i.e., subtracting the 
transformed symptoms at baseline from transformed symptoms 
at 2-­y follow-­up; see SI Appendix, Table S5; unstd B = 0.305, P 
= 0.001 for PV; unstd B = 0.351, P = 0.003 for FC; unstd B = 
0.059, P = 0.166 for PCDS).
 To further explore this moderation effect, we performed a simple 
slope analysis to assess the longitudinal relationship between each 
negative social context and MDD symptoms at four values of the 
left hippocampal volume: –2 SD from its mean, –1 SD, +1 SD, 
and +2SD. For youth with smaller left hippocampal volume (–2 
SD), the relationship between MDD symptoms and each of the 
three negative environments was statistically indistinguishable 
from zero (P > 0.100, solid red lines in Panels A–﻿C of  Fig. 2 ). 
Conversely, youth with larger left hippocampal volume (+2 SD), 
the longitudinal association between these variables was positive 
and statistically significant (P < 0.001, solid blue lines in Panels 
﻿A –C of  Fig. 2 ). The magnitude of these slopes for youth with 
relatively small left hippocampal volume (–1 SD) was between 6% 
and 26% of the slope magnitude for those individuals with large 
left hippocampal volume (+2 SD). The corresponding percentages 
were between 69% and 75% when comparing the slopes for youth 
with relatively large left hippocampal volume (+1 SD) with the 
slopes of those with large left hippocampal volume (+2 SD).

 To test the specificity by sex at birth, we estimated linear mixed 
models predicting MDD symptoms including the same predictors 
as before but also adding a three-way interaction between sex at

 To test the specificity of the moderation effect on MDD symp-
toms, we estimated linear mixed models separately predicting 
anxiety-related symptoms, psychotic-like experiences, and exter-
nalizing symptoms including the same predictors as above, but 
now adding youth symptoms and family history of the corre-
sponding mental health problem instead of depressive symptoms. 
Likewise, we used the corresponding caregiver symptoms as one 
of the negative social contexts we assessed, instead of caregiver’s 
symptoms of depression as well. Findings showed no moderation 
effects for any of these three outcomes or any of the negative social 
environments under study (SI Appendix, Table S8 ). 
Absence of Positive Experiences Affects Youth with Larger 
Left Hippocampal Volumes. We also examined whether the left 
hippocampal volume moderates the longitudinal association 
between MDD symptoms and two positive social contexts (i.e., PSE 
and PW) by separately including a two-­way interaction between 
left hippocampal volume × socio-­experiential environments in two 
independent linear mixed models predicting MDD symptoms 
[Columns (4) and (5) in SI  Appendix, Table  S2]. These two 
interactions were negative and statistically significant for prosocial 
school environments (unstd B = –0.348, P = 0.005) and parental 
warmth (unstd B = –0.637, P = 0.002). These results were robust 
to the exclusion of covariates (see SI Appendix, Table S3; unstd 
B = –0.327, P = 0.005 for PSE; unstd B = –0.492, P = 0.010 
for PW), conducting multiple imputation of missing values (see 
SI Appendix, Table S4; unstd B = –0.243, P = 0.064 for PSE; 
unstd B = –0.376, P = 0.045 for PW), and using the differences 
of the square root transformation of symptoms as the outcome 
(see SI Appendix, Table S5; unstd B = –0.115, P = 0.031 for PSE; 
unstd B = –0.226, P = 0.011 for PW).
 The simple slopes analysis for these two interactions revealed a 
stronger association between socio-experiential environments and 
MDD symptoms for youth with a larger left hippocampal volume 
and no differences in MDD symptoms between individuals with 
different sizes of left hippocampus at high levels of positive context 
exposure. Differences in MDD symptoms between youth with 
larger vs. smaller left hippocampal volume were observed for low 
values in the positive environment scales (see Panels D and E of 
 Fig. 2 ).
 Similar to the findings for adverse social contexts, the results 
for positive social environments showed no moderation effect from 
the right hippocampal volume when probed without controlling 
for the left hippocampal volume [see Columns (4) and (5) in 
﻿SI Appendix, Table S6 ; unstd B = –0.113, P = 0.339 for PSE; unstd 
B = –0.214, P = 0.251 for PW], opposite moderation effects when 
we control for left hippocampal volume (see SI Appendix, Table S7 ; 
unstd B = 0.409, P = 0.036 for PSE; unstd B = 0.533, P = 0.069 
for PW), no specificity of the left hippocampal volume modera-
tion effect across youth’ sex at birth ( Fig. 3 and SI Appendix, sec-
tion 8 ), and specificity of the moderation effect to MDD 
symptoms (SI Appendix, Table S8 ). 
The Moderation Effect Is Inconsistent with Alternative 
Interpretations. To increase the credibility of interpreting the left

hippocampal volume as a moderator of the association between 
social contexts and the development of MDD symptoms, we 
tested alternative conceptualizations. First, we assessed whether 
left hippocampal volume could be a mediator between socio-­
experiential environments and 2-­y change in MDD symptoms. 
A mediator is predicted by the variable of interest (i.e., social 
contexts) and predicts the outcome (i.e., 2-­y change in MDD 
symptoms). Consequently, we began by using linear mixed models 
to predict left hippocampal volume measured at baseline including 
the same predictors from our primary analysis. In this model, 
none of the five social contexts predicted left hippocampal volume 
after controlling for covariates (SI Appendix, Table S9). Moreover, 
we also tested whether the five socio-­experiential environments 
predicted the change in left hippocampal over 2 y. Using the same 
approach we used to test 2-­y change in MDD symptoms, we 
found no association between exposure to any of the five social 
contexts and changes in left hippocampal volume within 2 y 
(SI Appendix, Table S10).
 Next, we tested whether left hippocampal volume predicts 2-y 
change in MDD symptoms using a linear mixed model, including 
the same covariates as before. The results indicated that left hip-
pocampal volume measured at baseline predicted 2-y change in 
MDD symptoms, independently of the five social contexts exam-
ined in our study (see SI Appendix, Table S11 ; unstd B = 0.141, 
﻿P = 0.028). Taken together, these results suggest that left hip-
pocampal volume does not meet the criteria to be considered a 
mediator in the relationship between social contexts and MDD 
symptoms. However, a larger left hippocampal volume might 
predispose individuals to develop MDD symptoms over time.
 Second, we examined left hippocampal volume as a marker of 
MDD symptoms by assessing the concurrent association between 
these two variables. As shown in SI Appendix, Table S12 , left hip-
pocampal volume did not predict MDD symptoms when both 
were measured at baseline (unstd B = 0.060, P = 0.509). In addi-
tion, left hippocampal volume did not predict MDD symptoms 
when both were measured at 2-y follow-up (see SI Appendix, 
Table S13 ; unstd B = 0.089, P = 0.442).

demonstrate that depressive symptoms from retrospective reports 
at baseline on the period before the last 6 mo were uncorrelated 
with left hippocampal volume (unstd B = 0.001, P = 0.478). 
Exploring MDD Symptom Heterogeneity. Last, we explored 
MDD symptom heterogeneity by estimating linear mixed models 
predicting each of the 22 MDD symptoms independently. To this 
end, we conducted two sets of models. First, to assess the main 
effects, we included the same covariates from our main analysis 
but did not include an interaction between hippocampal volume 
and socio-­experiential environments (SI Appendix, Table S15). 
Despite the increase in measurement error compared to our

primary outcome measure combining all MDD symptoms into a 
single variable, the results showed statistical significance (P < 0.05) 
for almost all the longitudinal associations between the different 
socio-­experiential environments and each of the MDD symptoms. 
The estimates of these associations have the expected sign with 
negative environments positively related to MDD symptoms and 
positive environments negatively related to MDD symptoms.
 Second, to examine the moderation effects we included the 
covariates from our main analysis and an interaction term between 
left hippocampal volume and socio-experiential environments 
(SI Appendix, Table S16 ). Despite the increase in measurement 
error compared to our primary outcome measure combining all 
MDD symptoms into a single variable, this set of results suggests 
two patterns: i) across social contexts, the moderation effects 
seemed to emerge for more severe symptoms (e.g., wishes to be 
dead, suicidal ideation, causes impairment), and ii) the modera-
tion effect emerged for most MDD symptoms when analyzing 
peer victimization. 
Discussion
 Over the years, the pendulum has swung back and forth between 
approaches that have emphasized the importance of biological vs. 
environmental factors in the development of depression ( 73 ,  74 ). 
The present study adopted an interactionist perspective to eluci-
date the interplay between brain and environment in a critical 
developmental period—the transition to adolescence.
 Converging with past research, we found that negative social 
environments, such as peer victimization ( 75 ,  76 ), family conflict 
( 77 ,  78 ), and caregiver’s depressive symptoms ( 79 ,  80 ) predicted 
increases in adolescents’ depressive symptoms over 2 y. Similarly, 
the absence of positive social environments, such as prosocial 
school environment ( 81 ,  82 ) and parental warmth ( 83 ,  84 ) also 
predicted increases in adolescents’ depressive symptoms over time. 
To examine the interplay between brain and environment, we 
focused on the hippocampus as a critical brain region implicated 
in the development of depression ( 26 ,  27 ). Consistent with social 
sensitivity models ( 19 ,  20 ) and expanding upon prior research 
Schriber et al. ( 28 ), our findings showed that the hippocampus 
amplified sensitivity to different social contexts in a large-scale, 
US national, two-wave longitudinal study. Hippocampal volume 
consistently moderated these associations such that youth with 
larger left hippocampal volume experienced greater increases in 
depressive symptoms in more negative and less positive social 
environments, whereas adolescents with smaller left hippocampal 
volume were buffered against these adverse effects. Findings 
accounted for a host of covariates, including youth’s age, sex at 
birth, degree of pubertal development, education and cohabitating 
status of primary caregivers, family history of depression, and 
neighborhood social vulnerability. The moderation effect was not 
significantly different for individuals defined as boys or girls at 
birth, was specific to MDD symptoms (as it did not emerge for 
anxiety-related symptoms, psychotic-like experiences, and exter-
nalizing symptoms), and emerged most consistently across symp-
toms in direct negative experiences with peers (e.g., gets teased a 
lot) and for more severe symptoms of MDD (e.g., wishes to be 
dead). In addition, alternative explanations for the present findings 
(i.e., hippocampus as a mediator, marker of concurrent depression, 
or a sign of past depression) were not supported.
 The present findings converge with and expand upon previous 
research showing that a larger hippocampus confers greater social 
sensitivity in the development of MDD symptoms during ado-
lescence ( 28 ,  57 ,  85 ). Findings are also consistent with the role 
that the hippocampus plays in encoding contextual and social 
information from the environment ( 30 ,  32 ), its role in supporting 
other regions related to emotion regulation ( 21 ,  22 ,  29 ), and its 
role in the stress response system ( 33 ,  34 ,  51 ). The hippocampus 
has a high number of glucocorticoid receptors and mineralocor-
ticoid receptors, which allow the detection of circulating gluco-
corticoids and exert an inhibitory effect on the HPA axis to 
terminate the stress response and the secretion of cortisol ( 33 – 35 ). 
Accordingly, empirical evidence shows that adults who have devel-
oped depression typically exhibit hypersecretion of cortisol, 
impaired glucocorticoid receptor functioning, and reduced hip-
pocampal volumes ( 86 ,  87 ). A smaller adult hippocampus is a

robust result among clinical samples and has been related to expo-
sure to early adversity rather than directly linked with MDD ( 37 , 
 88 ), suggesting that hippocampal volumetric changes over the 
years could constitute an adaptive response to the quality of the 
environment. Importantly, the hippocampus changes rapidly in 
the first years of life, and environment-induced modifications 
might be more likely when the onset of adversity occurs before 
age five or several years after exposure ( 38 ,  89 ).
 Our results also demonstrate a left-lateralized effect, consistent 
with research across humans and animals. Extensive work in 
humans has demonstrated a link between reduced left hippocam-
pal volume in adults with higher levels of circulating cortisol 
( 90 – 93 ) and with a history of childhood maltreatment ( 6 ,  51 , 
 94 ). Similar asymmetries have been observed in NMDA receptors 
mediating the suppressive effects of glucocorticoids on hippocam-
pal neurogenesis ( 54 ,  55 ,  95 ) and the expression of corticosteroid 
receptors, which is greater in the left compared to the right hip-
pocampus ( 95 ). Converging evidence also comes from experimen-
tal work with animal models. For instance, Raineki et al. ( 53 ) 
induced maternal maltreatment of their pup rats by depriving 
them of sufficient nesting materials, which led to rough handling 
of pups and more maternal physical aggression. Compared to 
controls, this maltreatment resulted in increased levels of circu-
lating corticosterone and a smaller left (but not right) hippocampal 
volume. At the same time, maltreatment also affected pups’ social 
behavior, as they displayed lower attachment behaviors towards 
their mothers. Overall, these findings are in line with the motiva-
tional hypothesis, which postulates that the left hemisphere spe-
cializes in approach-related thoughts, whereas the right hemisphere 
controls avoidance-related thoughts ( 96 ). Although asymmetries 
or lateralization have repeatedly emerged in research probing hip-
pocampal function ( 6 ,  28 ,  52 ,  90 ,  93 ,  97 – 99 ), more research is 
still needed to uncover underlying sources and mechanisms.
 The hippocampus capacity for continued neurogenesis far into 
adulthood ( 95 ) and involvement in creating a mental model for 
the environment surrounding us ( 31 ) raises the possibility that 
this brain region is not only implicated in current stress reactivity 
( 20 ) but may also change and modify reactivity to future stress

( 100 ). This is consistent with a plastic adaptation view of the brain 
about the (expected) environment. Early adversity has been con-
sistently related to smaller adult hippocampal volume ( 6 ,  21 ,  22 , 
 36 – 38 ,  51 – 53 ), and such decreases in hippocampal volume may 
be adaptive after such adversity. The “change of pace” model sug-
gests that youth may experience delayed neural development fol-
lowing adversity, which may serve as a way to address gaps in the 
adverse environment ( 101 ). Delaying neural development lowers 
youth’s physiological needs in the contexts of resource deprivation 
and insecurity ( 102 ). Specifically, decreased hippocampus micro-
structure is linked to a reduction in abilities of information pro-
cessing and memory retention, which in turn might result in the 
relay of less contextual information to activate the subsequent 
amygdala response ( 62 ).
 Likewise, the left-lateralized enlargement reported of the hip-
pocampus after exposure to enriched environments ( 39 ) could be 
adaptive in facilitating positive youth development. For example, 
a larger hippocampus might be related to a higher capacity to 
integrate those positive contextual elements across space and time 
( 30 ,  103 ), which may benefit youth’s social and cognitive devel-
opment. Past studies suggest that a larger hippocampus may help 
improve youth’s understanding of social relationships ( 32 ,  104 ), 
increase their social engagement ( 42 ), and enhance their long-term 
memory functioning ( 105 ).
 Sensitivity to social contexts in the development of MDD 
symptoms does not necessarily imply overall vulnerability to social 
contexts in the development of other mental health problems. For 
instance, peer victimization has been linked to the development 
of multiple mental health problems including internalizing symp-
toms ( 75 ,  76 ,  106 ), psychotic-like experiences ( 107 ), and exter-

nalizing symptoms ( 108 ,  109 ). It is possible that while the 
hippocampus is a marker of vulnerability to developing MDD 
symptoms after exposure to adversity, other regions could be mark-
ers of vulnerability to developing other types of symptoms (e.g., 
psychotic-like experiences or externalizing symptoms, for which 
no hippocampal volume moderation effects emerged here) after 
exposure to the same type of adversity.
 The present study is based on a large sample and controls for a 
wide range of covariates. Still, it has some limitations. First, the 
current study was not preregistered ( 110 ). Therefore, we made 
available our Stata scripts to the research community to increase 
the transparency and replicability of this study. Second, focusing 
on late childhood before the typical emergence of MDD has the 
advantage of examining how early experiences shape later devel-
opment of MDD symptoms; however, it has the disadvantage of 
working with fewer individuals experiencing these symptoms 
( 111 ), which could reduce statistical power. Third, our focus on 
left (and right) hippocampal volume precludes us from a deeper 
analysis regarding subfield specificity. Recent studies have shown 
that different hippocampal subfields are implicated in different 
developmental processes, have distinguishable functions, and 
might be differentially responsive to the environment ( 6 ,  31 ,  52 , 
 105 ). Fourth, we did not explore potential interactions with other 
brain regions involved in the development of depressive symptoms 
such as the amygdala and the medial prefrontal cortex ( 112 ). A 
more comprehensive analysis has the potential to reveal interac-
tions between brain regions or circuits that are not possible to 
examine in more focused studies and would inform the discussion 
on time specificity of sensitive periods of development across brain 
regions ( 37 ). Fifth, our findings’ generalizability is limited to 
wealthier countries and likely does not represent societies with 
different MDD prevalence or levels of social stressors previously 
connected to individual’s exposure to negative socio-experiential 
environments such as poverty ( 113 ), lack of social cohesion ( 114 ), 
or economic inequality ( 115 ). Last, the longitudinal window cov-
ered in this study was 2 y. Studying wider time windows can 
inform to what extent the hippocampal volume responds to social 
environments and how persistent exposure to negative social con-
texts affects long-term adaptation via changes in hippocampal 
structure, function, and connectivity. 
Materials and Methods
Stata scripts used for data management and analyses for this manuscript are 
available in the online repository at GitHub: https://github.com/matmarti-­nu/
SEE-­LHV-­MDD.
Data. The present study used data from the ABCD study, which was designed to 
track the developmental trajectories of around 11,500 9-­ to 10-­y-­old youth living in 
21 cities across the United States (116, 117). Youth verbally consented to the study, 
their parents gave written informed consent, and each of the participating research 
site institutional review boards certified that the study complied with the biomedical 
ethics requirements involved in research with human subjects (118). The present 
analyses are based on the data at baseline and at 2-­y follow-­up (i.e., curated data 5.1).
The ABCD study recruited a sample of 11,832 youth and their primary 
caregivers in 21 cities in the United States. The baseline sample comprised 
9,668 single births, with 1,809 corresponding to siblings of other partici-
pants, 2,134 twins, and 30 triplets. For single births, sampling and recruit-
ment strategies usually involved recruiting 3rd and 4th-­grade students in 
randomly selected schools (116, 117). For twins and triplets, recruitment 
strategies relied on four centers with more than 30 y of experience conduct-
ing twin research (119).
Measures.
Symptoms of MDD. Symptoms of MDD were assessed at baseline and 2 y later 
using the computerized adaptation of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders 
and Schizophrenia for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 
Fifth Edition (KSADS-­5) (120, 121). Specifically, youth reported experiencing (0 = 
No, 1 = Yes) 22 symptoms during the last 6 mo: irritability, anhedonia, insomnia, 
fatigue, trouble concentrating, indecision, altered appetite, altered psychomotor 
presentation, guilt, hopelessness, lowered self-­esteem, self-­harm, suicidality, and

change in functioning related to these symptoms. As in prior research (122), we 
computed a sum score of the total number of items endorsed. Internal consistency 
was high with Cronbach’s alpha at baseline (α0) = 0.82 and Cronbach’s alpha at 
2-­y follow-­up (α2) = 0.84.
Social environments. Peer victimization was measured at baseline using the 
Peer Victimization subscale embedded in the social problems subscale of the 
Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), building on prior work (123–127). Specifically, 
caregivers reported on their child’s behavioral, social, and emotional problems 
(128, 129), including peer victimization with three items (i.e., gets teased a 
lot; not liked by other kids; does not get along with others; 0 = Not true; 1 = 
Somewhat or sometimes true; 2 = Very true or often true; α0 = 0.71; averaged).
Family conflict was measured at baseline using the Family Conflict subscale of 
the Family Environment Scale of the PhenX toolkit (130, 131). Specifically, youth 
reported on fighting, anger, criticism, competitiveness, and yelling within the 
family using nine items (0 = No, 1 = Yes; α0 = 0.70; averaged).
Caregiver’s depressive symptoms were measured using the Achenbach Adult 
Self-­report (ASR), which is one component of the Achenbach System of Empirically 
Based Assessment (ASEBA) (129, 132, 133). Caregivers reported 14 symptoms of 
depression in the past 6 mo (e.g., lack of energy, cries, suicidal thoughts, feeling 
worthless; 0 = Not true; 1 = Somewhat or sometimes true; 2 = Very true or often 
true; α0 = 0.84; averaged).
Prosocial school environment was measured using six items from the 
Inventory for School Risk and Protective Factor included in the ABCD study (134, 
135). Youth reported on opportunities and rewards for prosocial involvement in 
their schools (e.g., “In my school, students have lots of chances for students to 
get involved in sports, clubs, or other activities outside of class,” “In my school, 
students have lots of chances to help decide things like class activities and rules;” 
1 = NO!; 2 = no; 3 = yes; 4 = YES!–with capitalized responses meaning that 
the statement is definitely true for the child, and little letter if it is mostly true for 
them; α0 = 0.61; averaged).

Parental warmth was measured using the Acceptance Subscale of the Child 
Report of Behavior Inventory (CRPBI) (135, 136). Youth reported on parental 
warmth and acceptance of their primary caregiver using five items (e.g., makes 
me feel better after talking over my worries with him/her; 1 = Not like him/her; 
2 = Somewhat like him/her; 3 = A lot like him/her; α0 = 0.79; averaged).
Hippocampal volume. The ABCD study team developed a protocol for MRI acqui-
sition data aiming to maximize the comparability across research sites by drawing 
on previous big brain-­related data studies (137–139) and forming an Imaging 
Acquisition Workgroup in charge of harmonizing these data. This team defined 
a protocol harmonized for three 3T scanner platforms—Siemens Prisma, General 
Electric 750, and Philips—that use multichannel coils capable of multiband echo 
planar imaging acquisitions for a standard adult-­size coil. The following scanning 
parameters were used for T1 structural image acquisition: matrix = 256 × 256, 
176 slices, field of view (FOV) = 256 × 256, resolution (mm) = 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0, 
TR = 2,500 ms, TE = 2.88 ms, TI = 1,060 ms, flip angle = 8° (Siemens scanners); 
matrix = 256 × 256, 225 slices, FOV = 256 × 240, resolution (mm) = 1.0 × 1.0 
× 1.0, repetition time (TR) = 6.31 ms, echo time (TE) = 2.9 ms, inversion time

(TI) = 1,060 ms, flip angle = 8° (Phillips scanners); matrix = 256 × 256, 208 
slices, FOV = 256 × 256, resolution (mm) = 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0, TR = 2,500 ms, TE 
= 2 ms, TI = 1,060 ms, flip angle = 8° (GE scanners).
Participants’ brain scanning is performed in one or two sessions consisting 
of a fixed order of scan types beginning with a localizer, acquisition of 3D T1-­
weighted images, two runs of resting state fMRI, diffusion-­weighted images, 3D 
T2-­weighted images, one or two more runs of resting state fMRI, and task-­based 
fMRI (140). All the structural MRI data were processed using FreeSurfer in line 
with the standard processing pipelines. The process included the removal of 
nonbrain tissue, the segmentation of gray and white matter, and the parcellation 
of the cortical and subcortical structures. For quality control, the ABCD team first 
excluded participants according to automated quality control metrics of mean 
and SD of brain values and spatial signal-­to-­noise ratio. Then, the ABCD team 
manually inspected for signs of artifacts and poor image quality and manually 
reviewed FreeSurfer’s cortical surface reconstruction to gauge the severity of 
artifacts or processing problems. Following the ABCD team’s recommendations, 
we excluded 1,174 participants for quality control considerations. We separately 
computed the ratio between the left-­ and right-­hippocampal volumes to the 
intracranial volume.
Covariates. Covariates included youth’s age, sex at birth, race, lifetime exposure 
to traumatic events as a continuous score (141), degree of pubertal development 
using the Pubertal Development Scale at baseline by Petersen, Crockett, Richards 
and Boxer (142, 143), primary caregivers’ educational attainment, and whether 
the primary caregiver lived with a partner. We also included additional covari-
ates such as family history of depressive symptoms in first-­degree and second-­
degree relatives reported by the primary caregiver (144, 145), neighborhood 
impoverishment measured by an area deprivation index ranging from 1 to 100 
and validated for the U.S. by Singh (146, 147), which include 17 census poverty, 
education, housing, and employment indicators. See SI Appendix, Table S1 for 
descriptive statistics.
Other mental health symptoms, as alternative outcomes. Non-­depressive-­
internalizing (anxiety-­related) symptoms were assessed at baseline and 2 y later 
using the computerized adaptation of the KSADS-­5 (120, 121). Specifically, 
youth reported experiences of (0 = No, 1 = Yes) during the last 6 mo of seven 
symptoms of generalized anxiety (e.g., excessive worries more days than not; 
excessive worries across breadth of domains; difficulty controlling worries) and 
seven symptoms of social anxiety (e.g., fear of social situations; social situations 
invariably provoke anxiety; social fear is excessive for a given threat). We com-
puted a sum score of the total number of items endorsed. Internal consistency 
was high with Cronbach’s alpha at baseline (α0) = 0.91 and Cronbach’s alpha at 
the 2-­y follow-­up (α2) = 0.93.
Psychotic-­like experiences were collected at baseline and 2 y later using 
the distress score from the brief version of the Prodromal Questionnaire (148). 
Specifically, youth reported intensity of experiencing (1 = Yes, not very both-
ered; 2 = Yes, slightly bothered; 3 = Yes, moderately bothered; 4 = Yes, very 
much bothered; 5 = Yes, extremely bothered) 21 symptoms during the last 6 
mo (e.g., feels that someone else has taken control over the private thoughts; 
feels very certain that have magical talents). We used the average severity score 
of symptoms computed by ABCD team (as the ratio between their severity score 
and number of experienced symptoms) and included a zero for those who report 
not experiencing any symptoms (range 0 to 6). Internal consistency was high with 
Cronbach’s alpha at baseline (α0) = 0.86 and Cronbach’s alpha at 2-­y follow-­up 
(α2) = 0.86.
Externalizing symptoms were assessed at baseline and 2 y later using the

computerized adaptation of the KSADS-­5 (120, 121). Specifically, the primary 
caregiver reported youth’s experiences of (0 = No, 1 = Yes) 48 externalizing 
symptoms during the last 6 mo, with 18 related to ADHD (e.g., difficulty sustain-
ing attention; difficulty playing quietly), 15 to conduct disorder (e.g., has been 
physically cruel to people; often lies), and 8 to oppositional defiant disorder (e.g., 
often loses temper; spiteful or vindictive). We computed a sum score of the total 
number of items endorsed. Internal consistency was high with Cronbach’s alpha 
at baseline (α0) = 0.88 and Cronbach’s alpha at 2-­y follow-­up (α2) = 0.88.
Statistical Analysis. We began by studying the longitudinal associations 
between socio-­experiential variables measured at baseline and our outcome 
assessed 2 y later: MDD symptoms. Specifically, we followed prior theoretical 
and empirical research (71, 149–151) and regressed 2-­y change from baseline 
in MDD symptoms on MDD symptoms at baseline, our five variables of interest 
(i.e., peer victimization, family conflict, caregiver’s depressive symptoms, parental 
warmth, and prosocial school environment—separately in our main analysis, but 
also together as a robustness exercise in Fig. 1), left hippocampal volume (and 
right hippocampal volume in SI Appendix, section 6), and the set of covariates 
described above. We also included random intercepts by family and research 
sites to account for the clustering of the data. Models were fitted using multilevel 
mixed-­effects linear regression and the estimations were performed by maximum 
likelihood using the Stata command MIXED (152, 153).
We conducted three sets of sensitivity analyses to increase the credibility of 
the findings emerging from our main analysis. First, we tested the robustness 
of our main findings to potential overfitting induced by the inclusion of a large 
number of covariates (154, 155). To achieve this goal, we replicated our main 
analysis excluding the covariates described above (SI Appendix, Table S3). Despite 
the ABCD team intentionally developing a framework to increase retention (156), 
attrition and nonresponse for some variables resulted in listwise deletion anal-
yses based on a sample of around 8,100 when we included covariates (i.e., this 
number varies from 8,072 to 8,129 across the five SEE) and around 9,600 when 
we excluded the covariates (i.e., this number varies from 9,533 to 9,610 across 
the five SEE). Second, to avoid concerns related to potential nonrandom miss-
ingness due to attrition and nonresponse (157, 158), we replicated our main 
analysis using multiple imputation and conducted the analysis in ten complete 
databases (159, 160) (SI Appendix, Table S4). Third, to further reduce potential 
problems from the influence of potential outliers and skewness in the outcome 
variable (161, 162), we transformed depressive symptoms at baseline and 2-­y 
follow-­up by taking their square root and subtracted the former from the latter. 
Then, we used this variable as the outcome following the same approach as in 
our main analysis (SI Appendix, Table S5).
Next, we tested whether the left (and right) hippocampal volume moderated 
the longitudinal association between social contexts and MDD symptoms. The 
moderation analyses mirrored the multilevel strategy described above, including 
individually the left or right hippocampal volume, and adding all the covariates. 
In additional analyses, we tested the sensitivity of results by including both hip-
pocampal volumes in the same model (SI Appendix, Table S7). We also explored 
other potential relationships between our variables of interest. Specifically, fol-
lowing the work of Schreiber et al. (28), we tested whether the hippocampal 
volume operates as a mediator, state marker of depressive symptoms, or a scar 
of past depressive symptoms (SI Appendix, section 10).
Motivated by evidence suggesting higher prevalence of MDD symptoms (163, 
164) and larger hippocampal volumes (28) among girls, we tested whether the 
moderation effect of the hippocampal volume differed by the youth’s sex at birth. 
To achieve this goal, we added a three-­way interaction term between social con-

texts x hippocampal volume x sex at birth to the same multilevel model used for 
assessing the moderation effect (SI Appendix, section 8).
Finally, we explored the MDD symptom heterogeneity by replicating the 
moderation effect analysis using as outcome each of the 22 MDD symptoms 
(SI Appendix, section 11) and tested the specificity of the moderation effect to 
MDD symptoms by replicating the analysis using as outcome anxiety-­related 
symptoms, psychotic-­like experiences, and externalizing symptoms (SI Appendix, 
section 9). To test the moderation effects for these three outcomes, we used the
